Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)problematic paper screener

Problematic Paper Screener is an online platform, run by Guillaume Cabanac with Cyril Labbé and Alexander Magazinov since 27 February 2021, that screens the scientific literature for papers generated or disguised by tools and for references to retracted work, pairing machine detection with human assessment (MMRS record; arXiv:2210.04895).

🔎 What it detects

  • Tortured phrases: paraphrasing-tool output, "Joined Together States" for United States (The Conversation), "counterfeit consciousness" for artificial intelligence (Nature, quoted on its page).3↘
    The MMRS record calls it a set of detectors run over the literature: tortured phrases, SCIgen and Mathgen papers, references annulled or under concern, and others; the page's menu, updated 2026-10-28, lists ten (Annulled, Concerning, Feet of Clay, Tortured, Suspect, SCIgen, Mathgen, Citejacked, Seek&Blastn, Problematic Cell Lines), and The Conversation, in January 2025, counted eight beside tortured phrases, among them ChatGPT fingerprints, "snippets of telltale text left behind by the AI agent".§6 Tortured phrases are, in the makers' article, nonsensical word sequences found "littered throughout reputable scientific journals", which "typically result from using paraphrasing tools to evade plagiarism-detection software": "the Joined Together States" for the United States, the record's example too; the screener's page quotes Nature's post of 8 August 2021: "Why say 'colossal information' instead of big data? Or 'counterfeit consciousness' instead of artificial intelligence?"§7 The Capture Registry records the Overview's example of a tortured phrase, "counterfeit consciousness" for artificial intelligence, as the composition's, the record's being "Joined Together States", not checked against the screener's list; the example stands on the screener's own page, in Nature's post of 8 August 2021.§24
  • Generators: SCIgen and Mathgen papers; ChatGPT fingerprints.3↘
    The Problematic Paper Screener (PPS) is an online platform, in its makers' paper, that combines automatic machine detection with human assessment to identify and flag already published problematic articles (arXiv:2210.04895); its own page says it screens the scientific literature for papers (partly) generated with tortured phrases, SCIgen and Mathgen, and the MMRS record has it run by Guillaume Cabanac with Cyril Labbé and Alexander Magazinov since 27 February 2021, scanning the literature weekly for papers generated or disguised by tools and for references to retracted work, at the address dbrech.irit.fr.§1 The MMRS record calls it a set of detectors run over the literature: tortured phrases, SCIgen and Mathgen papers, references annulled or under concern, and others; the page's menu, updated 2026-10-28, lists ten (Annulled, Concerning, Feet of Clay, Tortured, Suspect, SCIgen, Mathgen, Citejacked, Seek&Blastn, Problematic Cell Lines), and The Conversation, in January 2025, counted eight beside tortured phrases, among them ChatGPT fingerprints, "snippets of telltale text left behind by the AI agent".§6 The same announcement describes the screener as a tool to identify and filter out articles "containing methodological errors, plagiarism, data manipulation, or conflicts of interest", a description that stands beside the screener's own list of detectors.§20
  • Feet of Clay: articles citing retracted, concerning or flagged references.2↘
    Its bibliographic detectors screen the articles citing retracted references, references marked with expressions of concern and references the screener's own detectors flag (its page), the one that finds articles citing retracted works named "Feet of Clay" (The Conversation); for a research question the MMRS record codes it as recording attribution partly, since references to retracted or concerning works are flagged.§8 By The Conversation's count it had found nearly 19,000 papers with at least five tortured phrases each, more than 280 SCIgen papers, more than 764,000 articles citing retracted works (about 5,000 with five or more), and more than 70 papers carrying ChatGPT fingerprints such as "Regenerate Response"; the MMRS record carries the same figures, dated "The Conversation, 31 January 2025", where the article at theconversation.com is dated 29 January 2025.§13
  • Detectors: ten on its menu (2026-10-28); nine in January 2025.3↘
    The MMRS record calls it a set of detectors run over the literature: tortured phrases, SCIgen and Mathgen papers, references annulled or under concern, and others; the page's menu, updated 2026-10-28, lists ten (Annulled, Concerning, Feet of Clay, Tortured, Suspect, SCIgen, Mathgen, Citejacked, Seek&Blastn, Problematic Cell Lines), and The Conversation, in January 2025, counted eight beside tortured phrases, among them ChatGPT fingerprints, "snippets of telltale text left behind by the AI agent".§6 Tortured phrases are, in the makers' article, nonsensical word sequences found "littered throughout reputable scientific journals", which "typically result from using paraphrasing tools to evade plagiarism-detection software": "the Joined Together States" for the United States, the record's example too; the screener's page quotes Nature's post of 8 August 2021: "Why say 'colossal information' instead of big data? Or 'counterfeit consciousness' instead of artificial intelligence?"§7 The same announcement describes the screener as a tool to identify and filter out articles "containing methodological errors, plagiarism, data manipulation, or conflicts of interest", a description that stands beside the screener's own list of detectors.§20

⚙️ How it works

  • Sources: Crossref with the Retraction Watch Database, Dimensions, PubMed, PubPeer.2↘
    Writing in The Conversation (29 January 2025) as "a pair of computer scientists at Université de Toulouse and Université Grenoble Alpes" who specialize in detecting bogus publications, Cabanac and Labbé say that Cabanac built the automated tool, and their disclosure names him its administrator: "a public platform that uses metadata from Digital Science and PubPeer via no-cost agreements".§4 It harvests the APIs of Crossref, "now including the Retraction Watch Database", Dimensions, PubMed and PubPeer (its page), the sources and intake the MMRS record states with the screener's page as basis.§9
  • Scale: 130 million papers a week.2↘
    It trawls "130 million scholarly papers every week" for signs of paper-mill production (The Conversation's standfirst, the article saying the same of Cabanac's tool), the weekly scan of 130 million publications the MMRS record gives as its cadence.§10 The archive's The Evaluator Exists (#741, 19 May 2026) reads the class the screener works on, paper-mill output, as proxy gaming at industrial scale, "thousands of fraudulent publications that enter the citation network and accumulate proxy signals indistinguishable from legitimate scholarship", holds that under the proxy regime "gaming is hard to detect because the signals being gamed are themselves opaque", and sets against it an evaluator that synthetic scholarship must get past by reading, with "empirical claims that survive a citation audit".§16
  • Review: machine detection with human assessment; flags reported on PubPeer.3↘
    The Problematic Paper Screener (PPS) is an online platform, in its makers' paper, that combines automatic machine detection with human assessment to identify and flag already published problematic articles (arXiv:2210.04895); its own page says it screens the scientific literature for papers (partly) generated with tortured phrases, SCIgen and Mathgen, and the MMRS record has it run by Guillaume Cabanac with Cyril Labbé and Alexander Magazinov since 27 February 2021, scanning the literature weekly for papers generated or disguised by tools and for references to retracted work, at the address dbrech.irit.fr.§1 Its makers start from the claim that post-publication assessment "remains necessary to check erroneous or fraudulent scientific publications" and present the screener as "a new effective tool to curate the scientific literature" (arXiv:2210.04895); Research Signals describes it as an academic project led by Cabanac and collaborators that "combines automatic machine detection and human evaluation".§11 "Problematic papers are reported on PubPeer" (its page).§12

📊 What it has found

  • By January 2025: nearly 19,000 tortured-phrase papers, 280+ SCIgen, 764,000+ citing retracted work, 70+ with ChatGPT fingerprints.2↘
    Its bibliographic detectors screen the articles citing retracted references, references marked with expressions of concern and references the screener's own detectors flag (its page), the one that finds articles citing retracted works named "Feet of Clay" (The Conversation); for a research question the MMRS record codes it as recording attribution partly, since references to retracted or concerning works are flagged.§8 By The Conversation's count it had found nearly 19,000 papers with at least five tortured phrases each, more than 280 SCIgen papers, more than 764,000 articles citing retracted works (about 5,000 with five or more), and more than 70 papers carrying ChatGPT fingerprints such as "Regenerate Response"; the MMRS record carries the same figures, dated "The Conversation, 31 January 2025", where the article at theconversation.com is dated 29 January 2025.§13
  • Retractions: more than 1,000 (its makers; MMRS record).1↘
    Several publishers use it, by its makers' account, some inside the editorial workflow to spot suspect papers upfront, and it "has been instrumental in more than 1,000 retractions"; analytics companies have used it to pick out suspect authors among highly cited researchers, Cabanac has offered pro bono consulting on detection tools to actors including ClearSkies, Morressier, River Valley, Signals and STM (The Conversation), and the MMRS record says it has contributed to more than 1,000 retractions.§17

⚖️ Limits

  • Iceberg: the fingerprinted papers are "the tip of the tip of the iceberg" (its makers).1↘
    Its makers state the limit of the fingerprint count themselves: those papers are "the tip of the tip of the iceberg", output "copy-pasted wholesale into papers without any editing (or even reading)", and "The challenge is to identify cases where chatbots are used not just for language-editing purposes but to generate content – essentially fabricating data."§14
  • Left out: "A detector finds what leaves a fingerprint"; clean machine text and real but misstated sources pass beneath it (MMRS record).1↘
    The MMRS record extends that limit to the whole instrument: "A detector finds what leaves a fingerprint", and "Text machine-written cleanly, or cited sources that exist but say something else, pass beneath it."§15
  • Proxy regime: paper-mill output gathers proxy signals "indistinguishable from legitimate scholarship" (#741).1↘
    The archive's The Evaluator Exists (#741, 19 May 2026) reads the class the screener works on, paper-mill output, as proxy gaming at industrial scale, "thousands of fraudulent publications that enter the citation network and accumulate proxy signals indistinguishable from legitimate scholarship", holds that under the proxy regime "gaming is hard to detect because the signals being gamed are themselves opaque", and sets against it an evaluator that synthetic scholarship must get past by reading, with "empirical claims that survive a citation audit".§16

🤝 Uptake

  • Signals Graph: over 12,000 unretracted flagged publications (June 2024).1↘
    On 20 June 2024 Research Signals integrated the articles it flags into the Signals Graph as a new signal, "over 12,000 problematic publications that have not been retracted", cited more than 160,000 times, to give sleuths, publishers and researchers visibility of them.§18
  • Episciences: references checked against its database of over a million (July 2026).2↘
    Its unit, in the MMRS record, is a published paper flagged by a detector; CCSD, announcing Episciences' adoption, describes what it provides as a database of over one million references identified as containing problematic elements, typed by severity from articles written entirely by AI to valid articles whose references carry anomalies ("Feet of clay").§2 On 3 July 2026 CCSD announced that Episciences analyses citations extracted from articles against the PPS database, at submission and after publication, displaying problematic citations for correction or information; of nearly 170,000 references in a first extraction, 226 were indexed in the PPS, most in the Feet of clay category.§19
  • Publishers: some in the editorial workflow (its makers).1↘
    Several publishers use it, by its makers' account, some inside the editorial workflow to spot suspect papers upfront, and it "has been instrumental in more than 1,000 retractions"; analytics companies have used it to pick out suspect authors among highly cited researchers, Cabanac has offered pro bono consulting on detection tools to actors including ClearSkies, Morressier, River Valley, Signals and STM (The Conversation), and the MMRS record says it has contributed to more than 1,000 retractions.§17

🧭 Place

  • Record: "the scholarly record's automated immune response", beside Academ-AI (MMRS record).1↘
    The MMRS record files it as a monitor and calls it "the scholarly record's automated immune response", the neighbour of Academ-AI, "which reads by phrase where the screener reads by detector"; with the screener, its Academ-AI record says, that database records "machine composition entering the scholarly record unattributed: the machine is the uncredited author, and the publisher is where the reception happens."§21

👁️ On the Overview

  • Recorded: the makers, sources and detectors right; the adoptions new to the record (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).2↘
    Google's AI Overview at the name, signed out, 2026-10-29, gave the three makers, the sources and the detectors as the IRIT page and the record give them, and composed the screener at its makers' grain, with its human review stage stated and its uptake by publishers' infrastructure added (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29, checked against the MMRS record and the entity's own pages); no card cited the record, which was published the same night.§23 The adoptions the Overview carried, Episciences and the Signals Graph, are uptake the MMRS record lacked (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); the rail's sixth card is Crossref's video "Exploring Retraction Watch Data in Crossref 2025-05-09", admitted by its title.§25

[QUERENT] problematic paper screener

[SYSTEM] The Problematic Paper Screener (PPS) is an online platform and automated screening tool developed by Guillaume Cabanac, Cyril Labbé, and Alexander Magazinov to detect fraudulent, error-filled, or computer-generated scientific literature. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESegHrOzAV8ssH4YuyzXH-7jZ7r8lC6wdexvCc9-qv_KPvpoq3ZevVQuluv6m4iFgagWOAzfdrjSDU9sBa4KnwCfM110wNvcA72Z6qELjoCCaGHCiRCuu9-XYqJWH-bItiV3x10sXCAtDY9zv0KgnnNBzC485GHu5AdaL-), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESWAHrOzAVdPdG6ZcwF_9hiFNiBbYAQmKr64ty8LbDt-8GilFnBTP7ja3lhKBrLFBF4D9Fy-amU5uCUNafRpaNJDrayo9BIOLRhai-oribmAcea0MqsmZMjyk)]
What It Detects
PPS scans millions of scholarly papers using data APIs (such as Crossref, Dimensions, PubMed, and PubPeer) across several specialized detectors: [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESpQEB6zswFYTNqhkmwOB_WpwElKixQzAgPEG430q65mypNNf9yrzASxZaXfauIKpghtOPsZvu6I289NGdwfTpFLF0cB57Cg2tbXOzmp3a9_sXWoaLcnrEhev2pFp36AiybcmCmgqdQMxavoLs3qzY8ZvBWbo_z9-wjZSuewyYuZi9SDbliJbm6Thpkxd43HJZbWves0EU79VqwjXH6CTf_13EUniGtyo), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESegHrOzAV8ssH4YuyzXH-7jZ7r8lC6wdexvCc9-qv_KPvpoq3ZevVQuluv6m4iFgagWOAzfdrjSDU9sBa4KnwCfM110wNvcA72Z6qELjoCCaGHCiRCuu9-XYqJWH-bItiV3x10sXCAtDY9zv0KgnnNBzC485GHu5AdaL-)]

* Tortured Phrases: Identifies nonsensical paraphrased terms (e.g., "counterfeit consciousness" instead of "artificial intelligence") used by paper mills to bypass plagiarism checkers. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESagHrOzAVdihLDpY-GrqzAs2cidfr9A6E0xEA5NsCdiT1k6bmGfNl4ZUfMvaXyXg3lDpaGPoWjW5VyXD8Ho7iBXaem40fdSQgVUj5HO5jPNKOK-BTrfzFiaAVyayoS8RpjlbjPPrsh5VbX0c), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESegHrOzAV8ssH4YuyzXH-7jZ7r8lC6wdexvCc9-qv_KPvpoq3ZevVQuluv6m4iFgagWOAzfdrjSDU9sBa4KnwCfM110wNvcA72Z6qELjoCCaGHCiRCuu9-XYqJWH-bItiV3x10sXCAtDY9zv0KgnnNBzC485GHu5AdaL-)]
* Computer-Generated Gibberish: Flags texts produced by automated paper generators like SCIgen and Mathgen. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESegHrOzAV8ssH4YuyzXH-7jZ7r8lC6wdexvCc9-qv_KPvpoq3ZevVQuluv6m4iFgagWOAzfdrjSDU9sBa4KnwCfM110wNvcA72Z6qELjoCCaGHCiRCuu9-XYqJWH-bItiV3x10sXCAtDY9zv0KgnnNBzC485GHu5AdaL-)]
* AI/LLM Fingerprints: Detects unedited AI-generated text patterns (such as ChatGPT remnants). [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESpQEB6zswFYTNqhkmwOB_WpwElKixQzAgPEG430q65mypNNf9yrzASxZaXfauIKpghtOPsZvu6I289NGdwfTpFLF0cB57Cg2tbXOzmp3a9_sXWoaLcnrEhev2pFp36AiybcmCmgqdQMxavoLs3qzY8ZvBWbo_z9-wjZSuewyYuZi9SDbliJbm6Thpkxd43HJZbWves0EU79VqwjXH6CTf_13EUniGtyo)]
* Feet of Clay (Retracted References): Tracks active or unretracted papers that improperly cite previously retracted works, expressions of concern, or withdrawn articles. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESegHrOzAV8ssH4YuyzXH-7jZ7r8lC6wdexvCc9-qv_KPvpoq3ZevVQuluv6m4iFgagWOAzfdrjSDU9sBa4KnwCfM110wNvcA72Z6qELjoCCaGHCiRCuu9-XYqJWH-bItiV3x10sXCAtDY9zv0KgnnNBzC485GHu5AdaL-), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESagHrOzAVdihLDpY-GrqzAs2cidfr9A6E0xEA5NsCdiT1k6bmGfNl4ZUfMvaXyXg3lDpaGPoWjW5VyXD8Ho7iBXaem40fdSQgVUj5HO5jPNKOK-BTrfzFiaAVyayoS8RpjlbjPPrsh5VbX0c)]

How It Works & Impact

* Combination Approach: It pairs automated machine-detection algorithms with human post-publication review. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESWAHrOzAVdPdG6ZcwF_9hiFNiBbYAQmKr64ty8LbDt-8GilFnBTP7ja3lhKBrLFBF4D9Fy-amU5uCUNafRpaNJDrayo9BIOLRhai-oribmAcea0MqsmZMjyk)]
* Reporting: Flagged papers are often automatically shared or logged on platforms like PubPeer and Pepia to alert editors, publishers, and the research community. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESegHrOzAV8ssH4YuyzXH-7jZ7r8lC6wdexvCc9-qv_KPvpoq3ZevVQuluv6m4iFgagWOAzfdrjSDU9sBa4KnwCfM110wNvcA72Z6qELjoCCaGHCiRCuu9-XYqJWH-bItiV3x10sXCAtDY9zv0KgnnNBzC485GHu5AdaL-), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESagHrOzAVdihLDpY-GrqzAs2cidfr9A6E0xEA5NsCdiT1k6bmGfNl4ZUfMvaXyXg3lDpaGPoWjW5VyXD8Ho7iBXaem40fdSQgVUj5HO5jPNKOK-BTrfzFiaAVyayoS8RpjlbjPPrsh5VbX0c)]
* Adoption: The tool has been integrated into editorial workflows, repository platforms (such as Episciences), and analytics frameworks (such as Signals Graph) to help scrub the scientific record of fabricated or corrupted studies. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESewHrOzAVdgRI6xW5dtQ02z6LRxaRnfusy1FeCyq8zi6RS1pJsOmxzZYHLttYgYLJFXU3eaKKVKJBkfSEu5hehC-0gdJN5kXqW9Y3WVrHFs5-H0illGRlauqKoBDO0ozdoe4U0vgz9vrt03Vz6ULeZAapK_OW7RrJcSCTtg), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESvAEB6zswFV-brn59UpZ0PxIrTzGUbqK7vxWA2X8DKXvY9zxXG1aJXnr9OcV8GXrmZkb6-s0nFnWBVL4S2cPTDL01B5-b1FZIIrkLOlhWF1jB3qkXkd283bVPGhddUaNWlQyLmlZyPz57TEARXfqDijOrk7ehNbsbEUGlY2ID8YPkBo2itUL3pMkjbRe6MTrO8fOJHqN2QFjaMkBdTBVYlfwAxkSCUe6QZ9pa3bDnLMMaRHtzHyXrVd9oN8eAbQ), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESpQEB6zswFYTNqhkmwOB_WpwElKixQzAgPEG430q65mypNNf9yrzASxZaXfauIKpghtOPsZvu6I289NGdwfTpFLF0cB57Cg2tbXOzmp3a9_sXWoaLcnrEhev2pFp36AiybcmCmgqdQMxavoLs3qzY8ZvBWbo_z9-wjZSuewyYuZi9SDbliJbm6Thpkxd43HJZbWves0EU79VqwjXH6CTf_13EUniGtyo)]

The Problematic Paper Screener

The Problematic Paper Screener (PPS) is an online platform, in its makers' paper, that combines automatic machine detection with human assessment to identify and flag already published problematic articles (arXiv:2210.04895); its own page says it screens the scientific literature for papers (partly) generated with tortured phrases, SCIgen and Mathgen, and the MMRS record has it run by Guillaume Cabanac with Cyril Labbé and Alexander Magazinov since 27 February 2021, scanning the literature weekly for papers generated or disguised by tools and for references to retracted work, at the address dbrech.irit.fr. Its unit, in the MMRS record, is a published paper flagged by a detector; CCSD, announcing Episciences' adoption, describes what it provides as a database of over one million references identified as containing problematic elements, typed by severity from articles written entirely by AI to valid articles whose references carry anomalies ("Feet of clay").

The page dates the screener "Est. February 27th, 2021" and gives its reference as Cabanac, Labbé and Magazinov (2022), presented at WCRI 2022, the 7th World Conference on Research Integrity; the paper was submitted to arXiv on 7 October 2022 by those three authors, and the MMRS record gives the same three as operator and the same founding date. Writing in The Conversation (29 January 2025) as "a pair of computer scientists at Université de Toulouse and Université Grenoble Alpes" who specialize in detecting bogus publications, Cabanac and Labbé say that Cabanac built the automated tool, and their disclosure names him its administrator: "a public platform that uses metadata from Digital Science and PubPeer via no-cost agreements". The page says it was "Featured in the Nature's 10 list of 2021"; The Conversation says it "was named one of 10 key developments in science by the journal Nature in 2021".

The MMRS record calls it a set of detectors run over the literature: tortured phrases, SCIgen and Mathgen papers, references annulled or under concern, and others; the page's menu, updated 2026-10-28, lists ten (Annulled, Concerning, Feet of Clay, Tortured, Suspect, SCIgen, Mathgen, Citejacked, Seek&Blastn, Problematic Cell Lines), and The Conversation, in January 2025, counted eight beside tortured phrases, among them ChatGPT fingerprints, "snippets of telltale text left behind by the AI agent". Tortured phrases are, in the makers' article, nonsensical word sequences found "littered throughout reputable scientific journals", which "typically result from using paraphrasing tools to evade plagiarism-detection software": "the Joined Together States" for the United States, the record's example too; the screener's page quotes Nature's post of 8 August 2021: "Why say 'colossal information' instead of big data? Or 'counterfeit consciousness' instead of artificial intelligence?" Its bibliographic detectors screen the articles citing retracted references, references marked with expressions of concern and references the screener's own detectors flag (its page), the one that finds articles citing retracted works named "Feet of Clay" (The Conversation); for a research question the MMRS record codes it as recording attribution partly, since references to retracted or concerning works are flagged.

It harvests the APIs of Crossref, "now including the Retraction Watch Database", Dimensions, PubMed and PubPeer (its page), the sources and intake the MMRS record states with the screener's page as basis. It trawls "130 million scholarly papers every week" for signs of paper-mill production (The Conversation's standfirst, the article saying the same of Cabanac's tool), the weekly scan of 130 million publications the MMRS record gives as its cadence.

Its makers start from the claim that post-publication assessment "remains necessary to check erroneous or fraudulent scientific publications" and present the screener as "a new effective tool to curate the scientific literature" (arXiv:2210.04895); Research Signals describes it as an academic project led by Cabanac and collaborators that "combines automatic machine detection and human evaluation". "Problematic papers are reported on PubPeer" (its page).

By The Conversation's count it had found nearly 19,000 papers with at least five tortured phrases each, more than 280 SCIgen papers, more than 764,000 articles citing retracted works (about 5,000 with five or more), and more than 70 papers carrying ChatGPT fingerprints such as "Regenerate Response"; the MMRS record carries the same figures, dated "The Conversation, 31 January 2025", where the article at theconversation.com is dated 29 January 2025.

Its makers state the limit of the fingerprint count themselves: those papers are "the tip of the tip of the iceberg", output "copy-pasted wholesale into papers without any editing (or even reading)", and "The challenge is to identify cases where chatbots are used not just for language-editing purposes but to generate content – essentially fabricating data." The MMRS record extends that limit to the whole instrument: "A detector finds what leaves a fingerprint", and "Text machine-written cleanly, or cited sources that exist but say something else, pass beneath it." The archive's The Evaluator Exists (#741, 19 May 2026) reads the class the screener works on, paper-mill output, as proxy gaming at industrial scale, "thousands of fraudulent publications that enter the citation network and accumulate proxy signals indistinguishable from legitimate scholarship", holds that under the proxy regime "gaming is hard to detect because the signals being gamed are themselves opaque", and sets against it an evaluator that synthetic scholarship must get past by reading, with "empirical claims that survive a citation audit".

Several publishers use it, by its makers' account, some inside the editorial workflow to spot suspect papers upfront, and it "has been instrumental in more than 1,000 retractions"; analytics companies have used it to pick out suspect authors among highly cited researchers, Cabanac has offered pro bono consulting on detection tools to actors including ClearSkies, Morressier, River Valley, Signals and STM (The Conversation), and the MMRS record says it has contributed to more than 1,000 retractions. On 20 June 2024 Research Signals integrated the articles it flags into the Signals Graph as a new signal, "over 12,000 problematic publications that have not been retracted", cited more than 160,000 times, to give sleuths, publishers and researchers visibility of them. On 3 July 2026 CCSD announced that Episciences analyses citations extracted from articles against the PPS database, at submission and after publication, displaying problematic citations for correction or information; of nearly 170,000 references in a first extraction, 226 were indexed in the PPS, most in the Feet of clay category. The same announcement describes the screener as a tool to identify and filter out articles "containing methodological errors, plagiarism, data manipulation, or conflicts of interest", a description that stands beside the screener's own list of detectors.

The MMRS record files it as a monitor and calls it "the scholarly record's automated immune response", the neighbour of Academ-AI, "which reads by phrase where the screener reads by detector"; with the screener, its Academ-AI record says, that database records "machine composition entering the scholarly record unattributed: the machine is the uncredited author, and the publisher is where the reception happens."

The MMRS record keeps itself apart from the entity, each assertion with a source and a basis and the lifecycle (active) apart from the observation (read, 2026-10-28); it read the screener's page for detectors, sources and start date, leaves the licence unchecked, and relates the capture of 2026-10-29 as the composition layer's account of the entity; the page itself was last updated on 2026-10-28 at 15:54.

Google's AI Overview at the name, signed out, 2026-10-29, gave the three makers, the sources and the detectors as the IRIT page and the record give them, and composed the screener at its makers' grain, with its human review stage stated and its uptake by publishers' infrastructure added (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29, checked against the MMRS record and the entity's own pages); no card cited the record, which was published the same night. The Capture Registry records the Overview's example of a tortured phrase, "counterfeit consciousness" for artificial intelligence, as the composition's, the record's being "Joined Together States", not checked against the screener's list; the example stands on the screener's own page, in Nature's post of 8 August 2021. The adoptions the Overview carried, Episciences and the Signals Graph, are uptake the MMRS record lacked (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); the rail's sixth card is Crossref's video "Exploring Retraction Watch Data in Crossref 2025-05-09", admitted by its title.

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)problematic paper screener

Problematic Paper Screener is an online platform that screens the scientific literature for papers partly generated with tortured phrases, SCIgen or Mathgen and for citations of retracted work, pairing machine detection with human assessment (its page; arXiv:2210.04895).

🔎 What it detects

  • Detectors: ten on its menu; tortured phrases from paraphrasing tools; ChatGPT fingerprints.2↘
    The page lists ten detectors and harvests Crossref with the Retraction Watch Database, Dimensions, PubMed and PubPeer, reporting problematic papers on PubPeer; the article counted nine, ChatGPT fingerprints among them, and a weekly trawl of 130 million papers for paper-mill output.§4 Tortured phrases come from paraphrasing tools used to evade plagiarism detection, as Joined Together States for United States, and Nature's post on the page gives counterfeit consciousness for artificial intelligence.§5
  • Sources: Crossref, Dimensions, PubMed, PubPeer; 130 million papers a week.1↘
    The page lists ten detectors and harvests Crossref with the Retraction Watch Database, Dimensions, PubMed and PubPeer, reporting problematic papers on PubPeer; the article counted nine, ChatGPT fingerprints among them, and a weekly trawl of 130 million papers for paper-mill output.§4

📊 Found and used

  • By January 2025: nearly 19,000 tortured-phrase papers; 764,000+ citing retracted work.1↘
    The article reports nearly 19,000 tortured-phrase papers, over 280 SCIgen papers, over 764,000 articles citing retracted work found by Feet of Clay, and over 70 with ChatGPT fingerprints, the last only the tip of the iceberg, with the open challenge of chatbots generating content.§6
  • Uptake: publishers, the Signals Graph, Episciences.2↘
    Publishers use it, some in the editorial workflow, it has helped toward more than 1,000 retractions, analytics firms have used it, and Cabanac consults pro bono for ClearSkies, Morressier, River Valley, Signals and STM.§7 Signals added over 12,000 unretracted flagged publications to its graph in June 2024; Episciences checks references against its database of over a million references in July 2026, finding 226 of nearly 170,000, describing it also as a filter for errors, plagiarism, manipulation and conflicts of interest.§8
  • Limit: fingerprints are the tip of the iceberg.1↘
    The article reports nearly 19,000 tortured-phrase papers, over 280 SCIgen papers, over 764,000 articles citing retracted work found by Feet of Clay, and over 70 with ChatGPT fingerprints, the last only the tip of the iceberg, with the open challenge of chatbots generating content.§6

Expansion · The field's ontology — L_F(B)9 sentences · every one sourced below

The Problematic Paper Screener

The Problematic Paper Screener screens the scientific literature for papers partly generated with tortured phrases, SCIgen or Mathgen and for bibliographies citing retracted, concerning or flagged references, by its own page, which dates it from 27 February 2021. Its makers' paper of 7 October 2022, by Cabanac, Labbé and Magazinov and presented at WCRI 2022, calls it an online platform pairing machine detection with human assessment to flag published problematic articles, since post-publication assessment remains necessary, and a tool to curate the literature; Research Signals calls it an academic project led by Cabanac.

Cabanac built it and administers it, using Digital Science and PubPeer metadata under no-cost agreements, in the account he and Labbé, computer scientists at Toulouse and Grenoble Alpes, gave The Conversation in January 2025; both the page and the article report its place in Nature's 10 of 2021.

The page lists ten detectors and harvests Crossref with the Retraction Watch Database, Dimensions, PubMed and PubPeer, reporting problematic papers on PubPeer; the article counted nine, ChatGPT fingerprints among them, and a weekly trawl of 130 million papers for paper-mill output. Tortured phrases come from paraphrasing tools used to evade plagiarism detection, as Joined Together States for United States, and Nature's post on the page gives counterfeit consciousness for artificial intelligence.

The article reports nearly 19,000 tortured-phrase papers, over 280 SCIgen papers, over 764,000 articles citing retracted work found by Feet of Clay, and over 70 with ChatGPT fingerprints, the last only the tip of the iceberg, with the open challenge of chatbots generating content.

Publishers use it, some in the editorial workflow, it has helped toward more than 1,000 retractions, analytics firms have used it, and Cabanac consults pro bono for ClearSkies, Morressier, River Valley, Signals and STM. Signals added over 12,000 unretracted flagged publications to its graph in June 2024; Episciences checks references against its database of over a million references in July 2026, finding 226 of nearly 170,000, describing it also as a filter for errors, plagiarism, manipulation and conflicts of interest.

The page was last updated 2026-10-28, and a Crossref webinar of 9 May 2025 on Retraction Watch data sits on the rail.

  • T1-1 definition: 'an online platform and automated screening tool developed by Guillaume Cabanac, Cyril Labbé, and Alexander Magazinov to detect fraudulent, error-filled, or computer-generated scientific literature'

L_F(B)recomposed from the disclosed field, in the field's ontology363 words

The Problematic Paper Screener screens the scientific literature for papers partly generated with tortured phrases, SCIgen or Mathgen and for bibliographies citing retracted, concerning or flagged references, by its own page, which dates it from 27 February 2021. Its makers' paper of 7 October 2022, by Cabanac, Labbé and Magazinov and presented at WCRI 2022, calls it an online platform pairing machine detection with human assessment to flag published problematic articles, since post-publication assessment remains necessary, and a tool to curate the literature; Research Signals calls it an academic project led by Cabanac. Cabanac built it and administers it, using Digital Science and PubPeer metadata under no-cost agreements, in the account he and Labbé, computer scientists at Toulouse and Grenoble Alpes, gave The Conversation in January 2025; both the page and the article report its place in Nature's 10 of 2021. The page lists ten detectors and harvests Crossref with the Retraction Watch Database, Dimensions, PubMed and PubPeer, reporting problematic papers on PubPeer; the article counted nine, ChatGPT fingerprints among them, and a weekly trawl of 130 million papers for paper-mill output. Tortured phrases come from paraphrasing tools used to evade plagiarism detection, as Joined Together States for United States, and Nature's post on the page gives counterfeit consciousness for artificial intelligence. The article reports nearly 19,000 tortured-phrase papers, over 280 SCIgen papers, over 764,000 articles citing retracted work found by Feet of Clay, and over 70 with ChatGPT fingerprints, the last only the tip of the iceberg, with the open challenge of chatbots generating content. Publishers use it, some in the editorial workflow, it has helped toward more than 1,000 retractions, analytics firms have used it, and Cabanac consults pro bono for ClearSkies, Morressier, River Valley, Signals and STM. Signals added over 12,000 unretracted flagged publications to its graph in June 2024; Episciences checks references against its database of over a million references in July 2026, finding 226 of nearly 170,000, describing it also as a filter for errors, plagiarism, manipulation and conflicts of interest. The page was last updated 2026-10-28, and a Crossref webinar of 9 May 2025 on Retraction Watch data sits on the rail.

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology1365 words

The Problematic Paper Screener (PPS) is an online platform, in its makers' paper, that combines automatic machine detection with human assessment to identify and flag already published problematic articles (arXiv:2210.04895); its own page says it screens the scientific literature for papers (partly) generated with tortured phrases, SCIgen and Mathgen, and the MMRS record has it run by Guillaume Cabanac with Cyril Labbé and Alexander Magazinov since 27 February 2021, scanning the literature weekly for papers generated or disguised by tools and for references to retracted work, at the address dbrech.irit.fr. Its unit, in the MMRS record, is a published paper flagged by a detector; CCSD, announcing Episciences' adoption, describes what it provides as a database of over one million references identified as containing problematic elements, typed by severity from articles written entirely by AI to valid articles whose references carry anomalies ("Feet of clay"). The page dates the screener "Est. February 27th, 2021" and gives its reference as Cabanac, Labbé and Magazinov (2022), presented at WCRI 2022, the 7th World Conference on Research Integrity; the paper was submitted to arXiv on 7 October 2022 by those three authors, and the MMRS record gives the same three as operator and the same founding date. Writing in The Conversation (29 January 2025) as "a pair of computer scientists at Université de Toulouse and Université Grenoble Alpes" who specialize in detecting bogus publications, Cabanac and Labbé say that Cabanac built the automated tool, and their disclosure names him its administrator: "a public platform that uses metadata from Digital Science and PubPeer via no-cost agreements". The page says it was "Featured in the Nature's 10 list of 2021"; The Conversation says it "was named one of 10 key developments in science by the journal Nature in 2021". The MMRS record calls it a set of detectors run over the literature: tortured phrases, SCIgen and Mathgen papers, references annulled or under concern, and others; the page's menu, updated 2026-10-28, lists ten (Annulled, Concerning, Feet of Clay, Tortured, Suspect, SCIgen, Mathgen, Citejacked, Seek&Blastn, Problematic Cell Lines), and The Conversation, in January 2025, counted eight beside tortured phrases, among them ChatGPT fingerprints, "snippets of telltale text left behind by the AI agent". Tortured phrases are, in the makers' article, nonsensical word sequences found "littered throughout reputable scientific journals", which "typically result from using paraphrasing tools to evade plagiarism-detection software": "the Joined Together States" for the United States, the record's example too; the screener's page quotes Nature's post of 8 August 2021: "Why say 'colossal information' instead of big data? Or 'counterfeit consciousness' instead of artificial intelligence?" Its bibliographic detectors screen the articles citing retracted references, references marked with expressions of concern and references the screener's own detectors flag (its page), the one that finds articles citing retracted works named "Feet of Clay" (The Conversation); for a research question the MMRS record codes it as recording attribution partly, since references to retracted or concerning works are flagged. It harvests the APIs of Crossref, "now including the Retraction Watch Database", Dimensions, PubMed and PubPeer (its page), the sources and intake the MMRS record states with the screener's page as basis. It trawls "130 million scholarly papers every week" for signs of paper-mill production (The Conversation's standfirst, the article saying the same of Cabanac's tool), the weekly scan of 130 million publications the MMRS record gives as its cadence. Its makers start from the claim that post-publication assessment "remains necessary to check erroneous or fraudulent scientific publications" and present the screener as "a new effective tool to curate the scientific literature" (arXiv:2210.04895); Research Signals describes it as an academic project led by Cabanac and collaborators that "combines automatic machine detection and human evaluation". "Problematic papers are reported on PubPeer" (its page). By The Conversation's count it had found nearly 19,000 papers with at least five tortured phrases each, more than 280 SCIgen papers, more than 764,000 articles citing retracted works (about 5,000 with five or more), and more than 70 papers carrying ChatGPT fingerprints such as "Regenerate Response"; the MMRS record carries the same figures, dated "The Conversation, 31 January 2025", where the article at theconversation.com is dated 29 January 2025. Its makers state the limit of the fingerprint count themselves: those papers are "the tip of the tip of the iceberg", output "copy-pasted wholesale into papers without any editing (or even reading)", and "The challenge is to identify cases where chatbots are used not just for language-editing purposes but to generate content – essentially fabricating data." The MMRS record extends that limit to the whole instrument: "A detector finds what leaves a fingerprint", and "Text machine-written cleanly, or cited sources that exist but say something else, pass beneath it." The archive's The Evaluator Exists (#741, 19 May 2026) reads the class the screener works on, paper-mill output, as proxy gaming at industrial scale, "thousands of fraudulent publications that enter the citation network and accumulate proxy signals indistinguishable from legitimate scholarship", holds that under the proxy regime "gaming is hard to detect because the signals being gamed are themselves opaque", and sets against it an evaluator that synthetic scholarship must get past by reading, with "empirical claims that survive a citation audit". Several publishers use it, by its makers' account, some inside the editorial workflow to spot suspect papers upfront, and it "has been instrumental in more than 1,000 retractions"; analytics companies have used it to pick out suspect authors among highly cited researchers, Cabanac has offered pro bono consulting on detection tools to actors including ClearSkies, Morressier, River Valley, Signals and STM (The Conversation), and the MMRS record says it has contributed to more than 1,000 retractions. On 20 June 2024 Research Signals integrated the articles it flags into the Signals Graph as a new signal, "over 12,000 problematic publications that have not been retracted", cited more than 160,000 times, to give sleuths, publishers and researchers visibility of them. On 3 July 2026 CCSD announced that Episciences analyses citations extracted from articles against the PPS database, at submission and after publication, displaying problematic citations for correction or information; of nearly 170,000 references in a first extraction, 226 were indexed in the PPS, most in the Feet of clay category. The same announcement describes the screener as a tool to identify and filter out articles "containing methodological errors, plagiarism, data manipulation, or conflicts of interest", a description that stands beside the screener's own list of detectors. The MMRS record files it as a monitor and calls it "the scholarly record's automated immune response", the neighbour of Academ-AI, "which reads by phrase where the screener reads by detector"; with the screener, its Academ-AI record says, that database records "machine composition entering the scholarly record unattributed: the machine is the uncredited author, and the publisher is where the reception happens." The MMRS record keeps itself apart from the entity, each assertion with a source and a basis and the lifecycle (active) apart from the observation (read, 2026-10-28); it read the screener's page for detectors, sources and start date, leaves the licence unchecked, and relates the capture of 2026-10-29 as the composition layer's account of the entity; the page itself was last updated on 2026-10-28 at 15:54. Google's AI Overview at the name, signed out, 2026-10-29, gave the three makers, the sources and the detectors as the IRIT page and the record give them, and composed the screener at its makers' grain, with its human review stage stated and its uptake by publishers' infrastructure added (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29, checked against the MMRS record and the entity's own pages); no card cited the record, which was published the same night. The Capture Registry records the Overview's example of a tortured phrase, "counterfeit consciousness" for artificial intelligence, as the composition's, the record's being "Joined Together States", not checked against the screener's list; the example stands on the screener's own page, in Nature's post of 8 August 2021. The adoptions the Overview carried, Episciences and the Signals Graph, are uptake the MMRS record lacked (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); the rail's sixth card is Crossref's video "Exploring Retraction Watch Data in Crossref 2025-05-09", admitted by its title.
